ready1_open_rewrite.title: PhysReason open-ended question
ready1_open_rewrite.rewritten_question_text: Two parallel, smooth inclined metal rails are spaced $L=0.2\mathrm{m}$ apart, with an angle of $\theta=37^{\circ}$ to the horizontal plane. A metal rod ab with a mass of $m=0.2\mathrm{kg}$ is placed perpendicularly on the rails. A uniform magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the rails. When a current $I=5\mathrm{A}$ flows from b to a through the rod, the rod can remain stationary on the inclined plane. Take $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, $\sin37^{\circ}=0.6$, and $\cos37^{\circ}=0.8$. 1. Determine the direction and magnitude of the magnetic induction $B$ of a uniform magnetic field; 2. If all other conditions remain unchanged, but the direction of the magnetic field is suddenly changed to vertically upward, and an external force $F$ is applied parallel to the rail direction to keep the metal rod stationary, determine the direction and magnitude of the external force $F$ acting on the metal rod.

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Two parallel, smooth inclined metal rails are spaced $L=0.2\mathrm{m}$ apart, with an angle of $\theta=37^{\circ}$ to the horizontal plane. A metal rod ab with a mass of $m=0.2\mathrm{kg}$ is placed perpendicularly on the rails. A uniform magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the rails. When a current $I=5\mathrm{A}$ flows from b to a through the rod, the rod can remain stationary on the inclined plane. Take $g=10\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, $\sin37^{\circ}=0.6$, and $\cos37^{\circ}=0.8$. 1. Determine the direction and magnitude of the magnetic induction $B$ of a uniform magnetic field; 2. If all other conditions remain unchanged, but the direction of the magnetic field is suddenly changed to vertically upward, and an external force $F$ is applied parallel to the rail direction to keep the metal rod stationary, determine the direction and magnitude of the external force $F$ acting on the metal rod.
ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: 1.2T, perpendicular to the slope upwards 0.24N, upward along the rail
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, there are two mutually parallel smooth metal guide rails forming an inclined plane, and the angle between the guide rails and the horizontal dashed line is labeled θ. The metal rod ab spans the two guide rails and is perpendicular to the direction of the guide rails; a and b are labeled at the two ends of the rod respectively. The magnetic field B is also marked in the figure, indicating that the magnetic field is perpendicular to the inclined plane where the guide rails are located. Reasoning: Take upward along the guide rails as the positive direction. The guide rails are smooth, and the rod is affected only by the component of gravity and the Ampere force in the direction along the guide rails. The component of gravity downward along the inclined plane is mg sinθ. It is known that the current goes from b to a. According to the right-hand rule, to make the rod remain at rest, the Ampere force I L × B must be upward along the guide rails, so the direction of the magnetic field should be perpendicular to the inclined plane upward. The equilibrium condition is BIL = mg sinθ, so B = mg sinθ/(IL) = 0.2×10×0.6/(5×0.2) = 1.2 T. In the second question, the magnitude of the magnetic field is still 1.2 T, but the direction is changed to vertically upward. The component of the vertically upward magnetic field relative to the normal direction of the inclined plane is B⊥ = B cosθ; only this component perpendicular to the plane of the guide rails makes the rod receive an Ampere force in the direction along the guide rails. This Ampere force is upward along the guide rails, with magnitude F_B = I L B cosθ = 5×0.2×1.2×0.8 = 0.96 N. The component of gravity downward along the guide rails is mg sinθ = 0.2×10×0.6 = 1.2 N. To keep it at rest, the external force needs to make up the upward force: F = 1.2 - 0.96 = 0.24 N, with direction upward along the guide rails.
